description: Hippocampus kuda, also known as the common seahorse, estuary seahorse, yellow seahorse, or spotted seahorse, is a species native to the Indian and Pacific Oceans. It has a completely monogamous mating system with elaborate courtship rituals — males change color patterns and dance around females while producing clicking sounds with the coronet. Females deposit up to 1,000 eggs into the male's ventral brood pouch via an ovipositor. Gestation lasts 20-28 days, with births typically occurring during a full moon. Newborn seahorses average 7 mm. They are omnivores feeding on larval fishes and zooplankton via suction feeding. Not strong swimmers, they spend most time anchored to seagrasses and corals with their tails.
population_estimate: Populations have declined by approximately 30% in the last few decades. Exact population numbers unknown, but still commonly encountered especially in Indonesia and New Guinea.
habitat: Found from the Persian Gulf to Southeast Asia, Australia, Japan, and several Pacific islands including Hawaii. Also found along the eastern coast of Africa from Tanzania to South Africa. Inhabits estuaries, lagoons, harbors, littoral zones, and coastal seagrass beds in shallow waters up to 55 meters depth. Majority of population along the Chinese coast down to Australia.
threats: Targeted catch for traditional Chinese medicine (25 million seahorses used annually)
Habitat destruction and degradation from pollution and coastal development
Low fecundity due to involved parental brood care method
ecosystem_role: Controls small crustacean and zooplankton populations through suction feeding. Serves as prey for crabs, rays, tuna, and sea turtles. Important indicator species for healthy coastal ecosystems, particularly seagrass beds and coral reefs. Contributes to the balance of plankton populations in their habitats.
human_connection: Extremely valuable in traditional Chinese medicine — said to regulate nervous, reproductive, endocrine, and immune systems. Largest exporters: Vietnam, India, Philippines, and Thailand. Popular in the aquarium trade, though they require specific care (72-77°F, pH 8.1-8.4, salinity ~32 ppt, quiet tanks with slow currents and anchor points). Listed in CITES Appendix II to regulate international trade.
what_students_can_do: Choose sustainably sourced captive-bred seahorses, not wild-caught for aquariums
Support marine protected areas that conserve seagrass habitats
Learn about sustainable fishing practices to reduce bycatch
Raise awareness about the impact of traditional Chinese medicine trade on seahorse populations
Reduce plastic pollution that degrades coastal and seagrass ecosystems
fun_fact: Male seahorses are the ones that get pregnant — they carry fertilized eggs in a brood pouch and give birth to live young!
They have a completely monogamous mating system — they mate for life and perform daily greeting dances with their partner
Despite being fish, they are terrible swimmers — they spend most of their time anchored to seagrass or corals with their prehensile tail
They can change color to match their surroundings for camouflage, much like chameleons
The species name 'kuda' means 'horse' in Malay — fitting for a creature named 'sea horse'!
